standard.title: Rules: who makes them and why they matter
standard.description: who makes rules, why rules are important in the school and/or the local community, and the consequences of rules not being followed
standard.strand: Knowledge and Understanding — Civics and Citizenship
standard.prior_knowledge: No direct prior HASS civics standard. Students have lived experience of rules from home and school.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain who makes rules, why rules are important, and describe the consequences of rules not being followed.

nodes.label: Who makes rules and why
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify who makes rules in different contexts (parents, teachers, coaches, councils) and explain why rules differ across contexts.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two rule-making authorities in different contexts and explain why each has that authority.
nodes.typical_width: Explore who has authority to make rules in different contexts (school, home, sport, community); consider why rules differ across contexts; examine cultural norms behind some rulemaking.
wider: Investigate how rules are made differently in different cultural contexts; for example, First Nations Australian cultural lore and how it governs community life
Research how community members can influence rule-making at school or local government level
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding who makes rules is prerequisite to explaining why specific rules exist — cause and consequence analysis requires knowing the source.

response_modes.reason: Rule-making authority is contextual and relational — use concrete scenarios from students' own experience before generalising.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: First Nations Australian customary lore provides a qualitatively different model of rule-making (oral, traditional, culturally embedded) that enriches understanding of why rules are created.
success_criteria: Names at least two rule-making authorities
Explains why each authority has the right to make rules in their context

nodes.label: Importance of rules and consequences
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain why rules are important (protecting rights, enabling fairness, maintaining safety) and describe consequences when rules are not followed.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain why at least one rule is important and describe at least one consequence of breaking it.
nodes.typical_width: Identify familiar rules; explain how rules protect the rights of others and define responsibilities; describe consequences of not following rules; discuss situations where one rule for all is unfair (e.g. students with disability).
wider: Develop and justify a set of fair rules for the class, considering different student needs
Discuss whether all rules are always fair and what should be done when a rule seems unfair

response_modes.reason: Connecting the importance of rules to the consequences of breaking them integrates authority, rights and responsibility into a coherent civics framework.

success_criteria: Explains why at least one rule is important
Describes at least one consequence of breaking a rule
